column4: The section's finish-then-act cycle is staged after Friday prayer: when it ends, spread through the land, seek Allah's bounty, and remember Him much.
After completing the pilgrimage rites, the verse commands remembrance of Allah; it directly matches the section's sequence of finishing one act and turning to the Lord.
After prayer is completed, remember Allah standing, sitting, and lying on your sides; the verse makes remembrance the next act and keeps it through every posture.
The section names the root ر غ ب for desire toward the Lord; after their garden is lost, its owners say إِنَّا إِلَىٰ رَبِّنَا رَٰغِبُونَ and hope He will replace it with something better.
The section's root ر غ ب is used in إِنَّا إِلَى ٱللَّهِ رَٰغِبُونَ: in a dispute over charity allotments, the proper answer is to desire Allah and accept His and His Messenger's giving.
The section's root ر غ ب appears in رَغَبًا وَرَهَبًا: Zakariya's household hastens to good deeds and calls on God with hope and fear, joining exertion to directed prayer.
The section's image of effort directed toward the Lord is stated as كَادِحٌ إِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ; the person strives toward his Lord and will meet Him.
After the long daytime occupation of 73:7, the Prophet is told to remember his Lord's name and تَبَتَّلْ إِلَيْهِ, devote himself wholly to Him, matching the section's redirection after work.
This neighbor names the day as a long occupation, which explains the section's pairing of daytime work with night devotion and turning to the Lord in 73:8.
The command قُمِ ٱلَّيْلَ calls the Prophet to rise for night worship, a concrete instance of the section's instruction to get up and exert oneself.
The Prophet is commanded قُمْ فَأَنذِرْ, rise and warn; it is one of the section's own examples of rising into a new task.
The next command in that address is ورَبَّكَ فَكَبِّرْ, to magnify the Lord, matching the section's directed stance after rising.
The same address ends this command sequence with وَلِرَبِّكَ فَٱصْبِرْ, be patient for your Lord; the action and its purpose are joined as in the section.
The command فَصَلِّ لِرَبِّكَ وَٱنْحَرْ directs both prayer and sacrifice to the Lord, giving a concrete form to the section's exclusive orientation.
The section's dictionary sense of ن ص ب includes setting oneself upright; قُومُوا لِلَّهِ قَٰنِتِينَ gives the related posture of standing devoutly for Allah.
Its phrase يَذْكُرُونَ ٱللَّهَ قِيَٰمًا وَقُعُودًا وَعَلَىٰ جُنُوبِهِمْ repeats the standing, sitting, and reclining remembrance named in 4:103, extending the section's all-posture turn to God.
Commerce and sale do not distract these people from Allah's remembrance, prayer, and giving; this concretizes the section's return to the Lord amid a long day's work.
This is the preceding stage of the Friday sequence completed in 62:10: leave trade when the call comes and hasten to Allah's remembrance before spreading out again.
After the Hajj remembrance in 2:200, this prayer asks for good in this world and the next; it specifies what a desire directed to God may seek.
The Hajj passage says أُو۟لَٰٓئِكَ لَهُمْ نَصِيبٌ مِّمَّا كَسَبُوا۟; the section's root ن ص ب also occurs here in the distinct sense of an allotted share, joined to what people earn.
The Hajj scene continues with وَٱذْكُرُوا۟ ٱللَّهَ فِىٓ أَيَّامٍ مَّعْدُودَٰتٍ, carrying remembrance beyond the completed rites into the following days.
This is the prayer immediately before the household described in 21:90: Zakariya asks his Lord not to leave him alone, making the next verse's hopeful and fearful calling concrete.
The preceding verse shows the charity critics pleased when given a share and angry when not; 9:59 answers that appetite with contentment in God's allotment and desire for Allah.
The verse after the charity response in 9:59 specifies the recipients of alms, locating the promised allotment in an actual distribution.
The section's garden owners are introduced as people tested through a garden; this is the scene whose loss later turns them toward their Lord in 68:32.
Before the loss, the owners resolve not to make an exception; that presumption contrasts with their later hope in the Lord's replacement in 68:32.
The garden's destruction comes as a visitation from their Lord while they sleep, adding divine ownership and provision to the scene that ends in their appeal.
The garden is left like a harvested field; this is the concrete loss behind the owners' later blame and hope for a better replacement.
The owners tell each other to go early to their crop if they intend to harvest it, supplying the labor and worldly aim behind the lost-garden scene.
On the way they resolve that no needy person should enter; this selfish plan contrasts with their later appeal to the Lord after the garden is gone.
One brother asks why they did not glorify God, identifying the neglected Godward response that frames their later confession and desire toward the Lord.
After the garden is lost they say سُبْحَٰنَ رَبِّنَا and admit wrongdoing; the scene moves from self-directed harvest to recognition of their Lord.
This is the mutual reproach explicitly mentioned in the section, immediately before the owners turn to their Lord in 68:32.
Their next words confess that they had transgressed; that admission makes their appeal for a better gift from their Lord in 68:32 a changed stance.
The garden episode closes by contrasting punishment in this life with the greater punishment of the Hereafter, widening the owners' lost worldly provision into an afterlife boundary.
The section's root ر غ ب for turning desire away occurs in Abraham's father's question أَرَاغِبٌ أَنتَ عَنْ ءَالِهَتِى; it is the opposite direction from the section's desire toward the Lord.
Abraham says he will separate from what they invoke besides Allah and call upon his Lord; this makes the turn away from idols in 19:46 a turn toward God.
Abraham's immediate reply to his father is that he will ask his Lord to forgive him, continuing the exchange from rejection of the idols toward appeal to the Lord.
The section's root ر غ ب in the sense of turning away appears in وَمَن يَرْغَبُ عَن مِّلَّةِ إِبْرَٰهِـۧمَ; the verse marks rejection of Abraham's way as the contrary orientation.
The section's root ف ر غ shifts subject: God says سَنَفْرُغُ لَكُمْ to the two weighty communities, a warning of His focused attention rather than a human being free to begin another task.
The section names ر غ ب and ن ص ب; here soldiers must not prefer their own lives over the Messenger, and the verse names thirst, نَصَب, and hunger in service of God.
The next verse records every small or large expense and every valley crossed for God's cause as a deed, showing effort directed to God and its recompense.
After the journey Moses says لَقَدْ لَقِينَا مِن سَفَرِنَا هَٰذَا نَصَبًا; this is the section's root ن ص ب in its fatigue sense, attached to purposeful travel.
The section itself cites عَامِلَةٌ نَّاصِبَةٌ, faces working and weary on the Day of Judgment; their exhausting labor is the image's contrast to effort deliberately turned toward the Lord.
The section's root ن ص ب for fatigue is reversed in the Garden: its people are not touched by نَصَب, so toil gives way to repose.
Here too the Garden's people say fatigue نَصَب does not touch them; the repeated absence of toil sharpens the section's picture of exertion in this life.
The command وَٱعْبُدْ رَبَّكَ حَتَّىٰ يَأْتِيَكَ ٱلْيَقِينُ makes devotion to the Lord continue until certainty comes, giving the section's new-work cycle an endpoint.
The section names the root ر ب ب and says all paths end with the Lord; وَأَنَّ إِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ ٱلْمُنتَهَىٰ states that destination directly.
The section's claim that return is to the Lord is directly phrased إِنَّ إِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ ٱلرُّجْعَىٰ.
The section defines the Lord as owner of every thing; this verse says وَهُوَ رَبُّ كُلِّ شَىْءٍ and then identifies the return to Him.
The section's dictionary branch for ر ب ب names blessing and goodness; this verse states that every نعمة people have is from Allah, clarifying the source of the gift they seek.
The Lord's abundant giving, named in the section's dictionary gloss for ر غ ب, has a direct promise here: وَلَسَوْفَ يُعْطِيكَ رَبُّكَ فَتَرْضَىٰ.
The section's root ر ب ب is joined to blessing in its dictionary gloss; this verse tells the Prophet to speak of the favor of his Lord, بِنِعْمَةِ رَبِّكَ.
This charity verse says spending is for oneself and only ابتغاء وجه الله; its promise of repayment connects work for others to a reward sought from Allah.
The people feed the needy, orphan, and captive; 76:9 explains that this concrete act is done only for Allah’s face, giving directed effort an example.
They say إِنَّمَا نُطْعِمُكُمْ لِوَجْهِ ٱللَّهِ and seek no reward or thanks, an explicit case of action oriented to God rather than human return.
The person gives his wealth to purify himself; 92:20 completes the motive as seeking his Lord’s face, paralleling effort aimed at God.
The section’s desire directed to the Lord is stated as إِلَّا ٱبْتِغَاءَ وَجْهِ رَبِّهِ ٱلْأَعْلَىٰ, a motive seeking the Lord’s face.
The section names ش ر ح from the opening of the breast; this verse uses يَشْرَحْ صَدْرَهُ لِلْإِسْلَٰمِ for a breast opened to Islam, specifying a Godward openness.
This repeats the section's ش ر ح / breast image as a chest Allah opens to Islam, contrasting inner light with mere worldly expansiveness.
Moses prays رَبِّ ٱشْرَحْ لِى صَدْرِى before undertaking his mission; the opened breast equips someone for the next task.
Moses follows the request in 20:25 with وَيَسِّرْ لِىٓ أَمْرِى, asking that his task be made easy; this continues the link between an opened breast and taking on work.
The other side of 17:18 desires the Hereafter and سَعَىٰ لَهَا سَعْيَهَا while believing; it joins directed desire to purposeful effort as the section does.
The counterpart fears standing before his Lord and restrains the soul from desire, وَنَهَى ٱلنَّفْسَ عَنِ ٱلْهَوَىٰ; it concretely joins reverence for the Lord to disciplining desire.
They explain the motive in 76:9 by saying they fear a day from their Lord, adding the accountability that guides their work.
The next verse says Allah protects them from that day’s evil, the divine care that answers their God-directed effort.
The passage concludes that Allah rewards their patience with a Garden and silk, showing the gift sought from the Lord after sustained effort.
This giving repays no favor from anyone, removing human reciprocity before the next verse names the Lord as its aim.
The final verse says this giver will be satisfied, completing the passage’s account of Godward work and its hoped-for outcome.
Its neighbor says the Hereafter is better and more enduring, completing the contrast to preferring worldly life in 87:16.
The next ayah adds that they leave the Hereafter, completing the immediate-life contrast of 75:20.
The next verse says the Lord knows best who has strayed from His way and who is guided, supplying the divine judgment on the worldly preference described in 53:29.
This neighbor gives the consequence of preferring worldly life: the blazing fire is the refuge.
This neighbor completes the contrast by naming the Garden as the refuge of the one who restrained desire before his Lord.
The section's root ن ص ب also appears in نَصِيبَكَ, one's share; this verse sets seeking the Hereafter beside not forgetting one's worldly share and doing good as Allah has done good.
The next ayah says they deny what they were given and enjoy themselves for a time, completing the reversal from gift to ingratitude in 16:54.
The same source-section root ش ر ح is used in مَن شَرَحَ بِٱلْكُفْرِ صَدْرًا, an opening of the breast toward disbelief, the contrary of the Godward opening in 94:1.
The section's root ن ص ب describes setting upright; this verse forbids meat sacrificed عَلَى ٱلنُّصُب, setting the erect cult stones against the section's prayer and sacrifice directed to the Lord.
The same section root ن ص ب appears as ٱلْأَنصَاب, erected stones for idolatrous rites; this marks a concrete boundary against directing worship anywhere but the Lord.
The verse contrasts a person who desires ٱلْعَاجِلَةَ and is given only what God wills with the section's desire aimed at the Lord; the outcome exposes the limit of seeking the immediate world.
At Badr, the believers are told تُرِيدُونَ عَرَضَ ٱلدُّنْيَا while Allah wills the Hereafter; this makes the section's warning against a broad worldly desire explicit.
After Uhud, the verse distinguishes among those who want worldly gain and those who want the Hereafter; it shows effort can be aimed in opposite directions.
The verse names preferring ٱلْحَيَوٰةَ ٱلدُّنْيَا, the opposite of the section's instruction to direct desire to the Lord.
The address says people love ٱلْعَاجِلَةَ, a specific counter-direction to the section's desire toward the Lord.
The person who turns away from God's remembrance and wants only worldly life, لَمْ يُرِدْ إِلَّا ٱلْحَيَوٰةَ ٱلدُّنْيَا, embodies the opposite stance to turning desire toward the Lord.
This person prefers worldly life, وَءَاثَرَ ٱلْحَيَوٰةَ ٱلدُّنْيَا, reversing the section's direction toward the Lord.
When harm is removed, the person continues as if he had never called Allah; this reverses the section's instruction to turn to the Lord after a difficulty or task has ended.
The person calls his Lord, دَعَا رَبَّهُ مُنِيبًا إِلَيْهِ, but forgets that prayer when given a blessing; the section's direction toward the Lord is set against forgetting Him after receiving good.
After Allah removes harm, a group associates others with their Lord; the verse reverses the section's exclusive turn toward Him after a change of circumstance.
In a storm at sea people call Allah sincerely, then the scene turns after rescue; this is a specific danger-and-relief setting for the change of orientation in 10:23.
After being saved to land, they commit injustice; the post-rescue turn away from God reverses the section's call to turn to Him after a completed ordeal.
At sea, distress leaves people calling only Allah, but once He saves them to land they turn away; this makes the section's post-relief orientation a clear boundary.
People aboard a ship call Allah sincerely, then associate others when He brings them safely to land; the reversal opposes the section's exclusive desire toward the Lord.

The verse sets people who call their Lord morning and evening, seeking His face, against one who wants the adornment of worldly life and follows desire; this closely meets the section’s turn from broad worldly longing to the Lord.
The parable begins with two men, one given two gardens; it is another concrete garden scene that frames the section’s lost-garden owners and their changed appeal to God.
The garden owner boasts that he has more wealth and followers, supplying the worldly confidence that contrasts with the section’s later appeal to the Lord after loss.

The boastful owner assumes that, if returned to his Lord, he will receive an even better return; this makes his expectation of worldly gain a false counterpart to the section’s humble hope in the Lord.
The other man says Allah is his Lord and he associates no one with Him, giving a direct contrasting stance within the same garden story.
The believing companion tells the owner to acknowledge Allah’s will and power when entering the garden, making the source of worldly provision explicit.
The companion says his Lord may give him a better garden and send a calamity upon the other; this anticipates the section’s garden owners hoping their Lord will replace what they lost.
The companion warns that the garden’s water could sink beyond recovery, naming the concrete limit on the owner’s apparent security.
After his garden is destroyed, the owner regrets that he associated anyone with his Lord; it is a close parallel to the section’s owners turning toward their Lord after losing a garden.
No faction can help the ruined owner against Allah, adding the collapse of worldly support to the garden-loss scene.
The passage concludes that true protection belongs to Allah and that He gives the best reward and outcome, identifying the Lord as the lasting source of support.
The command فَفِرُّوا إِلَى ٱللَّهِ directly names movement toward God, paralleling the section’s direction إِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ.
The next verse forbids setting another deity alongside Allah, making the exclusivity of fleeing toward Him explicit.
The Prophet is told to become upright toward God and seek His forgiveness; it joins an upright stance with a directed return to Him.
The command to set one’s face toward worship and call on God sincerely gives a concrete posture and act for the section’s exclusive Godward desire.
The Prophet says his prayer, sacrifice, life, and death are for Allah, Lord of the worlds; this gives the section’s direction toward the Lord a whole-life form.
The next verse adds that Allah has no partner and that this was commanded, sharpening the exclusivity stated in 6:162.
The verse says whoever hopes to meet his Lord should do righteous work and associate no one in worship with Him, joining effort, hope, and exclusive orientation.
People leave their beds to call their Lord in fear and hope and spend from what He provided; this brings rising, exertion, directed prayer, and divine provision into one image.
The next verse says no soul knows what comfort has been hidden for these workers as recompense for their deeds, connecting their effort to an abundant gift from God.
Those invoked besides God themselves seek access to their Lord, hope for His mercy, and fear His punishment; this explicitly describes desire directed toward the Lord with hope and fear.
The verse commands calling on the Lord in fear and hope, a repeated formulation of the posture described in 21:90.

The Prophet is told not to fix his eyes on worldly adornments given to others because his Lord’s provision is better and more lasting; this directly counters the section’s secondary image of broad desire for the world.
The next command is to keep the family at prayer and be patient in it, since Allah provides; it joins sustained effort in worship to provision from the Lord.
The Prophet is told to perform extra prayer at night in hope that his Lord will raise him to a praised station, joining night effort to hope in the Lord’s gift.
The righteous are described as sleeping little at night; this is another concrete night-devotion scene beside the section’s command to rise at night.
The same people seek forgiveness before dawn, completing the night-to-day devotion scene introduced in 51:17.
After help and victory arrive, the Prophet is told to glorify his Lord with praise and seek forgiveness; a completed mission turns directly into Godward action.

The verse says some people’s effort is lost in worldly life although they think they are doing good, a direct counterpart to the section’s warning that exertion can be wasted if it lacks the right direction.

The following verse says their deeds carry no weight on the Day of Resurrection because they rejected their Lord’s signs and meeting Him, supplying the reason and outcome for the lost effort in 18:104.
God promises not to waste any worker’s work, then names migration, expulsion, suffering, and struggle for His cause; it is the positive counterpart to labor that comes to nothing.
Those who recite the Book, establish prayer, and spend from God’s provision hope for a trade that will never fail, joining effort and worship to a lasting return.
The next verse says God will pay their wages in full and increase them from His bounty, specifying the gift behind their hoped-for return.
During the pilgrimage, people are to witness benefits and mention Allah’s name over the livestock He provided; it joins completed ritual, remembrance, and provision from God.
The next verse tells pilgrims to complete their rites, fulfill their vows, and circumambulate the Ancient House, extending the Hajj scene around the remembrance named in 22:28.
For every community a rite is appointed so they mention Allah’s name over the livestock He provided; the verse connects worship to gifts from the one God.
The sacrificial camels are made among God’s signs, and His name is mentioned over them; it gives a concrete form to sacrifice directed to the Lord.
The next verse says neither meat nor blood reaches Allah, but God-consciousness does; it clarifies that sacrifice’s Godward intention, not its material object, is what matters.
The verse contrasts one who wants the harvest of the Hereafter, whose yield God increases, with one who wants the harvest of this world; it joins work and the direction of desire.
Those who want worldly life and its adornment are paid for their deeds in this life but receive no share beyond it, a direct boundary on worldly-directed labor.
The next verse states their Hereafter outcome and that their deeds have come to nothing, completing the warning in 11:15.
Wealth and children are called adornment of worldly life, while lasting good deeds are better with the Lord as reward and hope; this gives a precise world-versus-enduring-work boundary.
After describing a sealed drink for the righteous, the verse says to let those who compete compete for it, redirecting aspiration toward an abundant divine gift.
The tranquil soul is called to return to its Lord, satisfied and accepted; this adds a personal return and satisfaction to the section’s claim that the destination is the Lord.
The address offers a trade that saves from painful punishment, setting up the section’s image of effort yielding a gift from God.
That trade is specified as faith and striving in Allah’s cause with wealth and lives, making exertion explicitly God-directed.
The following verse names forgiveness and Gardens as the return for that striving, completing the passage’s divine reward.
Allah is described as purchasing believers’ lives and property in exchange for the Garden; this concretely joins the Lord’s ownership, human effort, and abundant reward.
Before the address in 55:31, this verse says all in the heavens and earth ask God and He is each day in an affair, adding the ongoing divine activity behind the section’s use of farag for God.
The verse commands people to turn toward their Lord and submit to Him, directly paralleling the section’s direction إِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ.
